title:
Comment of John Keller in Docket(s)/Project(s) P-15423-000
Submission Date: 10/28/2026

documents.name: 151865.txt
documents.text:
John Keller, Stamford, CT.
I'm opposed to this project. DeepGreen is going to make life harder for the 331 remaining beluga whales in the Cook Inlet. They are already critically imperiled, and they are a high-priority species according to NOAA. Yet this project is proposed directly within their "critical habitat." 

In a five-year review, NOAA actually reported that several anthropogenic noise sources were found at levels with the potential to chronically mask beluga communication and hearing, and that shipping and dredging sounds exceeded behavioral-harassment levels daily in some monitored settings.

And that was found before a 100-megawatt data center right in the middle of their critical habitat was proposed.

Meanwhile, under the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), it is unlawful to take any marine mammal unless permitted by statutory exception. Take is defined as “to harass, hunt, capture, or kill, or attempt to harass, hunt, capture, or kill any marine mammal."

A study published in Frontiers found that thermal discharge from power plants can alter oxygen and pH levels and sediment composition, which ultimately reduces the number and variety of creatures that live nearby and on the seabed. The study also flagged increased heavy metals in one discharge scenario and research on how thermal discharge affects metal uptake in marine organisms.

And for a species like the beluga, with only an estimated 331 remaining in the Cook Inlet, the loss of even one Cook Inlet beluga whale should be considered devastating to the current population, as well as to the recovery of this magnificent species.

These cumulative impacts coalescing is what spells trouble. NOAA identifies “cumulative and synergistic stressors" as a "high-concern threat" to beluga recovery.
